tourism.title: Visitors and the people who live here
tourism.goal: Compare an article with an interview, distinguish benefits from costs and negotiate a fair visitor plan.
tourism.role: a representative chairing a fictional neighbourhood meeting about a tourist walking route
goals: Attribute two different interests accurately.
Use the interview to qualify an interpretation of the article.
Propose a feasible compromise and explain how to evaluate it.
tourism.opening: Our walking route brings visitors into the neighbourhood, but residents have raised concerns. What would a fair trial look like?

reading.prompt: What distinction is central to the proposal?
options: Charging every resident to leave home.
Closing all small shops to tourists.
Managing organised groups rather than banning all visitors.
reading.note: The booking proposal applies to large guided groups, not independent visitors.

reading.prompt: Why does Elena question a single visitor-count measure?
options: Local customers never use the area.
Passing foot traffic does not show how benefits are distributed.
Every business has already reported equal sales.
reading.note: She distinguishes movement through the area from purchases and access.

reading.prompt: Which response addresses both concerns?
options: Move explanations to a suitable space and provide accessible listening options.
Require Malik to change his working hours.
Remove all information for visitors who have difficulty hearing.
reading.note: The conflict concerns both location and access to information.

reading.prompt: What limitation should accompany the survey result?
options: It proves that exactly fifty residents live in the area.
It shows that everyone favours a complete ban.
Its timing and method may have excluded relevant groups.
reading.note: An accessible sample can still leave important perspectives unrepresented.

reading.prompt: What would paying the fee allow an operator to do?
options: Ignore stopping-place rules whenever a guide prefers.
Use the booking system subject to the shared-space rules.
Prevent residents from using a public street.
reading.note: A fee does not purchase exclusive control of the street.

reading.prompt: Which evaluation best matches the article?
options: Combine access, resident, business and visitor evidence.
Count only how many tour tickets were sold.
Treat silence from residents as proof that no problems exist.
reading.note: The proposed evaluation considers several groups and reporting conditions.

listening.prompt: Which rule applies even below the booking threshold?
options: Every independent visitor must pay a fee.
Small groups can reserve a doorway for their guide.
Groups must not stop at private entrances.
listening.note: The threshold affects booking, not the shared-space rule.

listening.prompt: How should the garden proposal be described?
options: Rejected by Malik because he opposes all visitors.
Supported as a possibility, with access and scheduling checks outstanding.
Confirmed for every tour throughout the year.
listening.note: Support for a trial location is not a completed booking.

listening.prompt: Why test the receivers with different visitors?
options: One device may not meet every hearing need.
The purchase has already been completed.
Receivers would give guides private ownership of the garden.
listening.note: The equipment is a possible tool, not a universal solution.

listening.prompt: How will the new survey responses be used?
options: As a replacement that makes all earlier responses invalid.
As proof that only night workers live in the neighbourhood.
Alongside the earlier responses, with collection methods explained.
listening.note: Different samples can add perspectives without automatically cancelling each other.

listening.prompt: What should operators tell customers about arriving late?
options: Late groups can always enter together with the next booking.
A later slot may be unavailable, so an alternative route may be necessary.
A later slot is guaranteed without contacting anyone.
listening.note: Retain the conditional nature of the booking desk’s offer.

listening.prompt: What concern should the final report check?
options: Whether the plan displaced problems onto other people or places.
Whether every business sold exactly the same products.
Whether visitor totals can replace all other evidence.
listening.note: A local improvement may conceal a new problem elsewhere.

roleplay.prompt: The tour company says that more visitors must benefit every shop. How would you respond?
options: More visitors prove every shop earns the same amount.
The repair shop cannot have any relevant experience.
We should compare purchases and access across different businesses, not just total foot traffic.
roleplay.note: Use Elena’s distinction between passing people and distributed benefits.
roleplay.sceneLine: The tour company says that more visitors must benefit every shop. How would you respond?

roleplay.prompt: Malik wants quiet, and a visitor needs help hearing. What compromise would you explore?
options: Tell Malik that earning money removes his right to complain.
An accessible stopping place with tested listening equipment.
Tell the visitor to attend without understanding the guide.
roleplay.note: A compromise considers both needs rather than dismissing one.
roleplay.sceneLine: Malik wants quiet, and a visitor needs help hearing. What compromise would you explore?

roleplay.prompt: Can we tell guides that the garden is confirmed?
options: Not yet; access and existing bookings still need checking.
Yes, because one resident supports trying it.
No public garden can ever be used by a tour.
roleplay.note: Do not turn provisional support into permission.
roleplay.sceneLine: Can we tell guides that the garden is confirmed?

roleplay.prompt: A group of twelve wants to explain the route at a private doorway. What do you say?
options: Groups below fifteen have no responsibilities.
Only the residents need to book a time slot.
The booking threshold does not remove the rule against blocking entrances.
roleplay.note: Separate the size threshold from the access rule.
roleplay.sceneLine: A group of twelve wants to explain the route at a private doorway. What do you say?

roleplay.prompt: Our late group asks for a guaranteed later slot. How would you answer?
options: We should join another group without telling the guide.
We can ask the desk, but may need another route if no slot is available.
I guarantee a space before checking with staff.
roleplay.note: Be helpful while retaining the actual limit.
roleplay.sceneLine: Our late group asks for a guaranteed later slot. How would you answer?

roleplay.prompt: The main street is quieter, but a side street now has queues. What should the meeting recommend?
options: Review the route and include the people affected by the new queues.
Declare success because the main street improved.
Remove the side-street comments from the report.
roleplay.note: Check displacement rather than selecting only favourable evidence.
roleplay.sceneLine: The main street is quieter, but a side street now has queues. What should the meeting recommend?

checkpoint.prompt: Which interpretation of the proposed fee is justified?
options: It guarantees that every business will profit.
It funds administration; it does not grant control over public streets.
It allows operators to exclude residents.
checkpoint.note: The article explicitly limits what payment means.

checkpoint.prompt: A guide says a group of fifteen must book. Which correction follows the interview?
options: All groups of any size require a booking.
Exactly fifteen people may block an entrance.
The proposed threshold is more than fifteen, while entrance rules still apply.
checkpoint.note: Retain both the threshold and the general access condition.

checkpoint.prompt: Why would a lower complaint count need cautious interpretation?
options: Some affected people may not know how to report a problem.
Complaints are the same as sales receipts.
Fewer complaints prove every visitor heard the guide.
checkpoint.note: The reporting process affects what a complaint count can show.

checkpoint.prompt: What additional evidence would support a garden stopping place?
options: A promise that equipment will suit every visitor without testing.
A completed access check and confirmation that the space is available.
Only a guide’s preference for the scenery.
checkpoint.note: Both availability and access remain unresolved.

checkpoint.prompt: Which finding would challenge the claim that benefits are shared evenly?
options: A resident submitting a paper survey.
Strong sales at one stop but reduced local access elsewhere.
A guide using an agreed stopping place.
checkpoint.note: Look at distribution rather than the total number passing through.

checkpoint.prompt: Which final recommendation best reflects both sources?
options: Try clear booking rules, consult affected groups and check whether problems move elsewhere.
Confirm every proposed detail before checking it.
Use only tour-ticket sales to decide success.
checkpoint.note: Combine practical rules, source limitations and a review process.

readingPoints: Managing organised groups rather than banning all visitors.
Passing foot traffic does not show how benefits are distributed.
Move explanations to a suitable space and provide accessible listening options.
Its timing and method may have excluded relevant groups.
Use the booking system subject to the shared-space rules.
Combine access, resident, business and visitor evidence.
listeningPoints: Groups must not stop at private entrances.
Supported as a possibility, with access and scheduling checks outstanding.
One device may not meet every hearing need.
Alongside the earlier responses, with collection methods explained.
A later slot may be unavailable, so an alternative route may be necessary.
Whether the plan displaced problems onto other people or places.

work.title: A fair experiment with flexible work
work.goal: Interpret a workplace trial, separate outcomes from assumptions and negotiate workable team arrangements.
work.role: a fictional team coordinator discussing a hybrid-work trial with an employee
goals: Explain both a benefit and an operational constraint.
Distinguish the recorded figures from a causal claim.
Agree on a fair arrangement and a review measure.
work.opening: Our team is considering a flexible-work trial. Which parts could improve your work, and which responsibilities need a shared plan?

reading.prompt: What would the trial change?
options: The service would close on two weekdays.
Everyone would have to give up the office.
Where some work happens, rather than the total working hours.
reading.note: The proposal changes location while preserving working hours and service coverage.

reading.prompt: Why does Dana want continued office access?
options: The trial would require a longer commute every day.
Home is not always a suitable place for focused work.
She wants to stop writing customer responses.
reading.note: Her support for flexibility includes a realistic fallback.

reading.prompt: What is Tomas’s main concern?
options: Maintaining reliable support for new starters.
Proving that every remote employee works less.
Removing all online contact between colleagues.
reading.note: He is discussing training arrangements, not making a general accusation.

reading.prompt: Why is the pilot insufficient to establish a causal effect?
options: No one completed any requests during the pilot.
A four-week observation automatically proves a permanent improvement.
Participants selected themselves and the requests may differ in difficulty.
reading.note: Selection and task differences offer alternative explanations.

reading.prompt: Which arrangement supports both flexibility and coordination?
options: Allowing availability to remain unknown until someone asks.
A shared availability plan with a named contact and a change process.
Publicly sharing customer details to explain every delay.
reading.note: The agreement makes contact and changes predictable without exposing private information.

reading.prompt: What would a balanced review consider?
options: Quality, support and different working conditions alongside case totals.
Only the largest individual output figure.
Only the views of people with ideal home offices.
reading.note: The proposed review combines output with quality and fairness.

listening.prompt: What does “up to two days” mean here?
options: Every employee must work remotely for exactly two days.
The office will close for two days.
Employees may choose fewer remote days or none.
listening.note: The adjustment preserves a choice rather than imposing a fixed pattern.

listening.prompt: Why publish a shared training day?
options: To remove the named online contact.
So new starters know when mentors will be available together.
To make every team use identical days permanently.
listening.note: The arrangement makes support predictable while allowing changes.

listening.prompt: Which expectation does the coordinator reject?
options: That remote staff must remain available all evening.
That the existing service schedule still matters.
That urgent issues need an agreed procedure.
listening.note: Working remotely does not create unlimited availability.

listening.prompt: Why record support given to colleagues?
options: Training colleagues proves that no customer work was done.
Only people with the highest raw total may train others.
Case totals alone can miss an employee’s training contribution.
listening.note: The comparison must account for different kinds of work.

listening.prompt: What is the first step after a connection problem?
options: Post customer account details on a public page.
Inform the named contact and discuss a practical response.
Pretend to be available until the working day ends.
listening.note: The priority is timely communication followed by a suitable arrangement.

listening.prompt: What distinction matters when interpreting problems?
options: Failure of a particular arrangement is not automatically failure of every flexible model.
Any positive comment proves the trial works for everyone.
Any delay means remote work can never work anywhere.
listening.note: The coordinator avoids overgeneralising in either direction.

roleplay.prompt: I support remote work, but home is noisy on some days. What could we agree?
options: Require everyone to stay home regardless of conditions.
Treat access needs as evidence of poor motivation.
Keep office access available and discuss changes in advance.
roleplay.note: A flexible arrangement should include a workable alternative.
roleplay.sceneLine: I support remote work, but home is noisy on some days. What could we agree?

roleplay.prompt: New starters cannot find anyone to help. What would you propose?
options: Assume that lower case totals prove mentors are not working.
Publish shared training days and name an online contact.
Tell new starters to guess who might answer.
roleplay.note: Make the support responsibility explicit.
roleplay.sceneLine: New starters cannot find anyone to help. What would you propose?

roleplay.prompt: The pilot group completed more cases. Can we say remote work caused it?
options: We need to consider experience and case complexity before making that claim.
Yes, a higher average rules out every other explanation.
No observation from a pilot can ever be useful.
roleplay.note: Useful evidence can still be insufficient for a causal conclusion.
roleplay.sceneLine: The pilot group completed more cases. Can we say remote work caused it?

roleplay.prompt: A colleague wants to measure commitment by evening message replies. How do you respond?
options: Everyone must stay online until the last customer sleeps.
Remote days remove all service responsibilities.
Let us use agreed hours and work evidence, not constant online visibility.
roleplay.note: Keep work obligations within the agreed schedule.
roleplay.sceneLine: A colleague wants to measure commitment by evening message replies. How do you respond?

roleplay.prompt: My connection is failing and another team is waiting. What should I say?
options: I can promise uninterrupted access without checking.
I am having a connection problem; can we agree on an alternative for today?
I will say nothing until the team complains.
roleplay.note: A specific update helps others plan.
roleplay.sceneLine: My connection is failing and another team is waiting. What should I say?

roleplay.prompt: Output increased but mentors report heavier workloads. What should the review do?
options: Examine training and support distribution alongside output and quality.
Ignore mentors because total cases increased.
Assume every employee has exactly the same tasks.
roleplay.note: Fair evaluation includes contributions and costs beyond one number.
roleplay.sceneLine: Output increased but mentors report heavier workloads. What should the review do?

checkpoint.prompt: What do both accounts preserve despite changing the work location?
options: A requirement for evening replies from everyone.
A guarantee of exactly two remote days for every employee.
Existing working hours and reliable service coverage.
checkpoint.note: Location and working-time obligations are separate.

checkpoint.prompt: What should an employee do when home conditions are unsuitable?
options: Leave the team without an availability update.
Claim that the trial permanently closes the office.
Discuss using the office rather than assuming it is unavailable.
checkpoint.note: The revised plan retains office access.

checkpoint.prompt: Which evidence would make the pilot comparison more informative?
options: Online status alone.
Only the most enthusiastic participant’s opinion.
Case difficulty, response quality and support contributions.
checkpoint.note: The article identifies important missing variables.

checkpoint.prompt: Why might a mentor complete fewer customer cases?
options: The total proves that the mentor did no useful work.
The policy forbids mentors from answering customers.
Some working time may be spent supporting new colleagues.
checkpoint.note: Different responsibilities can produce different raw counts.

checkpoint.prompt: Which conclusion goes beyond the evidence?
options: The volunteers’ positive experience proves that every employee benefits.
The pilot offers observations worth examining.
Different home conditions should be considered.
checkpoint.note: Self-selected experiences do not represent everyone.

checkpoint.prompt: A shared schedule causes repeated support gaps. What is a proportionate response?
options: Check the arrangement and test a revision before generalising to every model.
Hide the support gaps because the trial is popular.
Declare all flexible working impossible without examining the cause.
checkpoint.note: Evaluate implementation and outcome separately.

readingPoints: Where some work happens, rather than the total working hours.
Home is not always a suitable place for focused work.
Maintaining reliable support for new starters.
Participants selected themselves and the requests may differ in difficulty.
A shared availability plan with a named contact and a change process.
Quality, support and different working conditions alongside case totals.
listeningPoints: Employees may choose fewer remote days or none.
So new starters know when mentors will be available together.
That remote staff must remain available all evening.
Case totals alone can miss an employee’s training contribution.
Inform the named contact and discuss a practical response.
Failure of a particular arrangement is not automatically failure of every flexible model.

food.title: Good food, fewer leftovers
food.goal: Follow a food-surplus project, interpret quantities carefully and negotiate a reliable collection plan.
food.role: a coordinator of a fictional community food-sharing project discussing a collection pilot
goals: Explain a practical benefit and a safety constraint.
Interpret the interview’s changes to collection arrangements.
Propose a reliable plan without overstating the evidence.
food.opening: We want to reduce good food going to waste, but the collection plan must be reliable. Which part should we organise first?

reading.prompt: What is the pilot designed to use?
options: A guaranteed number of extra meals cooked for the project.
Every item regardless of its condition.
Suitable food that remains unsold, in variable quantities.
reading.note: The project uses surplus rather than guaranteeing new production.

reading.prompt: Why is a box count insufficient?
options: The number of collections can never be recorded.
Boxes may contain different amounts and types of food.
Every box contains exactly one complete meal.
reading.note: A container count does not establish a standard quantity of meals.

reading.prompt: Who would decide which café items are suitable to share?
options: Café staff following the relevant handling procedures.
A passer-by choosing items without information.
Any volunteer guessing from the appearance alone.
reading.note: The plan assigns the suitability decision to staff rather than improvisation.

reading.prompt: Which arrangement protects recipients’ privacy?
options: Ask everyone to explain their finances publicly.
Publish a named list alongside collection photographs.
Record distribution totals without publishing recipients’ names.
reading.note: The proposed data collection concerns the service rather than public personal details.

reading.prompt: How should the five-collection figure be interpreted?
options: As a guarantee of identical food supplies every evening.
As a plan depending on volunteer availability.
As a record of five completed collections.
reading.note: An estimate of capacity is not an observed outcome.

reading.prompt: Why might fewer donated items be a positive result?
options: Better preparation planning may have prevented surplus.
It necessarily means volunteers stopped attending.
It proves the community no longer needs support.
reading.note: Donation volume alone cannot show whether waste increased or decreased.

listening.prompt: How will the third café be handled?
options: It is already confirmed for all four weeks.
Its totals will be counted as if it joined on the first day.
It may join later, and the report will show its actual participation period.
listening.note: A possible later start must remain distinct from confirmed participation.

listening.prompt: What should a delayed volunteer do first?
options: Assume the food can wait indefinitely.
Contact the café and backup promptly.
Collect whenever convenient without telling anyone.
listening.note: Timely communication allows the agreed procedure to operate.

listening.prompt: What can the centre reasonably promise?
options: Information about expected distribution, with updates if it changes.
A complete reserved meal for everyone who asks.
The same food selection every evening.
listening.note: The service can communicate reliably even when supply varies.

listening.prompt: What qualification should accompany the portion count?
options: Every counted portion is a verified complete meal.
It establishes exactly how much each person ate.
It is an estimate using a stated counting method.
listening.note: A defined estimate remains different from direct measurement of consumption.

listening.prompt: Which distinction does the coordinator make?
options: No organising team may know how to contact its volunteers.
Private volunteer contact details and public distribution reporting serve different purposes.
All personal details should be published together.
listening.note: Collect and disclose information according to its specific purpose.

listening.prompt: What is needed before interpreting a lower donation total?
options: Evidence about collections, leftovers and preparation changes.
An immediate conclusion that the project failed.
An assumption that every recipient stopped coming.
listening.note: Several processes can produce the same donation figure.

roleplay.prompt: A poster says everyone can reserve a complete meal. How should we revise it?
options: Keep the guarantee because it will attract more people.
Promise identical meals from every café.
Describe the expected distribution time and explain that items and quantities vary.
roleplay.note: Reliable communication should match the actual service.
roleplay.sceneLine: A poster says everyone can reserve a complete meal. How should we revise it?

roleplay.prompt: The third café wants to join in week two. What should the rota show?
options: No difference between a possible start and a confirmed one.
The confirmed start date and the collections it can actually support.
Four weeks of completed collections before they happen.
roleplay.note: Record actual participation rather than assumed coverage.
roleplay.sceneLine: The third café wants to join in week two. What should the rota show?

roleplay.prompt: I am running late for tonight’s collection. What should I do?
options: Contact the café and backup now and follow the agreed collection window.
Arrive whenever possible without an update.
Ask café staff to leave unlabelled food outside overnight.
roleplay.note: A safe plan requires communication and limits.
roleplay.sceneLine: I am running late for tonight’s collection. What should I do?

roleplay.prompt: Can we publish recipients’ names to show the project’s success?
options: Yes, public names are necessary to count every item.
Only volunteers can decide to disclose another person’s finances.
We can report distribution totals without identifying recipients.
roleplay.note: Service evidence does not require a public recipient list.
roleplay.sceneLine: Can we publish recipients’ names to show the project’s success?

roleplay.prompt: The final week has fewer donated portions. What should we investigate?
options: Whether we can hide that week from the report.
Whether preparation, surplus or collection reliability changed.
Whether one smaller number proves every aim failed.
roleplay.note: Investigate alternative explanations and report the method.
roleplay.sceneLine: The final week has fewer donated portions. What should we investigate?

roleplay.prompt: How would you sum up the trial’s aim at the meeting?
options: Share suitable surplus reliably and learn how to prevent avoidable waste.
Keep donation boxes full by asking cafés to cook extra.
Measure success only by the number of photographs posted.
roleplay.note: Redistribution and prevention can support the wider purpose in different ways.
roleplay.sceneLine: How would you sum up the trial’s aim at the meeting?

checkpoint.prompt: Which result could indicate successful waste prevention?
options: Lower surplus after cafés improve preparation planning.
More extra food cooked only to fill donation boxes.
A higher box count without any information about contents.
checkpoint.note: The article distinguishes preventing surplus from redistributing it.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should the cafés’ totals include participation dates?
options: All three cafés have already joined for the same period.
Dates prove that every container holds an identical meal.
A café joining later has had fewer collection opportunities.
checkpoint.note: Compare exposure periods as well as totals.

checkpoint.prompt: What should a volunteer do with an unlabelled item?
options: Ask the responsible café staff rather than guess suitability.
Distribute it because good intentions remove the need for checks.
Ask a recipient to decide without any information.
checkpoint.note: Responsibility and handling instructions matter.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the portion estimate not establish?
options: That the team used a described counting method.
That quantities can vary between collections.
Exactly how much each individual consumed.
checkpoint.note: A distribution estimate is not a direct consumption measure.

checkpoint.prompt: Which reporting choice follows the privacy plan?
options: Link every recipient’s name to their personal finances.
Replace distribution records with identifiable photographs.
Publish useful totals while keeping recipients’ identities private.
checkpoint.note: Separate operational records from public reporting.

checkpoint.prompt: A collection is missed. Which response is justified?
options: Record it and investigate its cause alongside the other results.
Treat the missing food as proof that no café produced surplus.
Erase the missed collection to improve the published total.
checkpoint.note: Preserve the record and avoid inventing a cause.

readingPoints: Suitable food that remains unsold, in variable quantities.
Boxes may contain different amounts and types of food.
Café staff following the relevant handling procedures.
Record distribution totals without publishing recipients’ names.
As a plan depending on volunteer availability.
Better preparation planning may have prevented surplus.
listeningPoints: It may join later, and the report will show its actual participation period.
Contact the café and backup promptly.
Information about expected distribution, with updates if it changes.
It is an estimate using a stated counting method.
Private volunteer contact details and public distribution reporting serve different purposes.
Evidence about collections, leftovers and preparation changes.

heat.title: Cooling a city without hiding the trade-offs
heat.goal: Synthesize a policy article and an interview, distinguish measurements from lived exposure and negotiate an equitable pilot.
heat.role: a chair of a fictional city working group considering a heat-reduction pilot
goals: Distinguish the study’s measured outcome from a wider policy claim.
Represent competing access and maintenance needs without dismissing either.
Propose an equitable pilot with explicit evidence limits and review criteria.
heat.opening: We have a promising cooling proposal, but the evidence and the distribution of benefits need scrutiny. What would you want the pilot to establish?

reading.prompt: Which revision would make the announcement more defensible?
options: Describe the measured surface difference as the long-term exposure benefit expected across the city.
Describe the nearby untreated section as evidence that every alternative intervention is unnecessary.
Describe the measured surface difference without claiming a proven reduction in personal exposure.
reading.note: The demonstration measured a particular outcome; a wider human-exposure claim needs additional evidence.

reading.prompt: What does the reviewer’s recommendation seek to improve?
options: The assumption that weather and existing shade have identical effects everywhere.
The basis for attributing an observed difference to the intervention.
The wording used to treat all existing observations as automatically invalid.
reading.note: Better comparisons address plausible alternative explanations without erasing useful observations.

reading.prompt: Why might pedestrian totals distort the priority ranking?
options: They can overlook prolonged exposure among fewer people at waiting places.
They directly measure how long every pedestrian spends waiting without shade.
They establish that all shopping journeys carry a greater individual heat burden.
reading.note: Counts of movement do not necessarily capture duration, vulnerability or waiting conditions.

reading.prompt: Which comparison is most consistent with the article?
options: Compare options only on the amount of shade visible at the installation ceremony.
Compare new trees with mature structures while treating maintenance as an identical fixed cost.
Compare options over time, including their maintenance and changing shade coverage.
reading.note: A fair comparison needs consistent time horizons and explicit operational assumptions.

reading.prompt: What would the proposed reporting method make clearer?
options: Which reported preference must be treated as a direct sensor reading.
Which claims come from measurements, reported experiences or interpretation.
Which individual residents follow a particular daily route to each monitored stop.
reading.note: Transparent categories preserve the different evidential status of different observations.

reading.prompt: Which final recommendation preserves the article’s reasoning?
options: Run a proportionate pilot that reports distributions, drawbacks and grounds for revision.
Roll out the intervention city-wide once the average surface reading shows any improvement.
Postpone all practical testing until every possible individual outcome is known in advance.
reading.note: The article supports a bounded, informative decision under uncertainty rather than either extreme.

listening.prompt: What distinction is the reviewer insisting on?
options: A lower surface reading establishes the same benefit for every journey.
A policy ambition becomes a measurement once it appears in a summary.
A desired journey-level benefit is not yet the demonstrated outcome.
listening.note: The speaker separates the intended benefit from the outcome actually observed.

listening.prompt: How will the original comparison be treated?
options: Given the same evidential weight as every new point regardless of conditions.
Retained with its limitations, while other comparisons help address specific questions.
Discarded because adding a comparison makes earlier observations inherently false.
listening.note: Retention and evidential weight are separate decisions.

listening.prompt: Which qualification must accompany the clinic-stop plan?
options: Its temporary structure still requires permission despite the decision to include the stop.
Its selection proves that it has the highest pedestrian count in the city.
Its access consultation removes the need for any remaining site permission.
listening.note: A selected priority is not the same as secured installation permission.

listening.prompt: What response to conflicting evidence does the reviewer favour?
options: Replace all sensor records with interview comments whenever the two differ.
Treat every resident report as mistaken because it is not a temperature reading.
Investigate what each measure captures and retain the discrepancy in reporting.
listening.note: Different measures can concern different aspects of the experience.

listening.prompt: What remains unresolved in the funding plan?
options: Whether removing a structure automatically funds its maintenance beforehand.
Maintenance funding and responsibility, separate from fitting and removal.
The entire installation budget, which the coordinator says does not exist.
listening.note: A capital or installation allocation does not establish ongoing operational provision.

listening.prompt: What evaluation practice does the reviewer reject?
options: Choosing a favourable outcome afterwards and presenting it as the original success criterion.
Publishing review criteria before the intervention begins.
Recommending a revised intervention after examining mixed results.
listening.note: Pre-specified criteria reduce selective interpretation of mixed findings.

roleplay.prompt: A draft headline says that our treatment has solved residents’ heat exposure. How would you revise it?
options: The demonstration proves long-term exposure benefits across all comparable neighbourhoods.
The surface comparison establishes that no additional exposure measurements are relevant.
The demonstration found lower surface readings; journey-level exposure still needs assessment.
roleplay.note: Match the claim to the measured outcome.
roleplay.sceneLine: A draft headline says that our treatment has solved residents’ heat exposure. How would you revise it?

roleplay.prompt: The busiest shopping street wins under our pedestrian-count rule. What might that rule miss?
options: A journey count already includes each person’s waiting duration and access needs.
Fewer people may face longer exposure while waiting at an unshaded stop.
Every quieter location must have a lower individual exposure burden.
roleplay.note: A distributional argument can change what should be counted.
roleplay.sceneLine: The busiest shopping street wins under our pedestrian-count rule. What might that rule miss?

roleplay.prompt: The clinic stop is a priority. Can we announce that installation is confirmed?
options: We should explain the outstanding permission and maintenance arrangements.
Priority status means that site permission and operational funding are complete.
Consultation replaces the need to identify anyone responsible for maintenance.
roleplay.note: Separate a policy priority from delivery conditions.
roleplay.sceneLine: The clinic stop is a priority. Can we announce that installation is confirmed?

roleplay.prompt: Residents’ reports and sensors disagree. Which next step would you defend?
options: Discard resident reports so that the report contains only one consistent story.
Substitute reported comfort for every sensor measure without further examination.
Check timing and what each measure captures, then report both accounts with their limits.
roleplay.note: Preserve discrepant evidence and investigate the reason for it.
roleplay.sceneLine: Residents’ reports and sensors disagree. Which next step would you defend?

roleplay.prompt: Someone argues that no action is justified until uncertainty disappears. How would you respond?
options: An appealing average justifies city-wide installation without monitoring alternatives.
A bounded pilot can be justified if it is proportionate and designed to resolve relevant uncertainty.
Any uncertainty makes all temporary experiments as unjustifiable as a permanent rollout.
roleplay.note: Distinguish a proportionate test from an irreversible commitment.
roleplay.sceneLine: Someone argues that no action is justified until uncertainty disappears. How would you respond?

roleplay.prompt: Please propose one condition for continuing the pilot.
options: Continue only with clear maintenance responsibility and a review that includes disadvantaged routes.
Continue automatically if one selected temperature measure improves at any point.
Continue while withholding difficult findings until the permanent contract is signed.
roleplay.note: A defensible condition combines delivery and evidence rather than publicity.
roleplay.sceneLine: Please propose one condition for continuing the pilot.

checkpoint.prompt: Which finding would most directly address the article’s exposure gap?
options: Additional installation photographs from the same favourable afternoon.
A larger total of pedestrians without information about their time in each place.
Measurements of actual journeys and waiting conditions alongside the surface readings.
checkpoint.note: The missing outcome concerns lived exposure rather than surface temperature alone.

checkpoint.prompt: Why are the extra comparison points useful without being perfect matches?
options: They establish identical conditions merely by increasing the number of sensors.
They can examine particular alternative explanations while leaving residual uncertainty explicit.
They make every previous observation false by introducing new locations.
checkpoint.note: Usefulness does not require pretending that all comparison conditions are identical.

checkpoint.prompt: Which budget claim would overstate the plan?
options: Ongoing care needs a named arrangement as well as installation funding.
Different time horizons affect the comparison between shade options.
Fitting and removal funding guarantees that maintenance is already funded.
checkpoint.note: The article and interview distinguish installation from ongoing provision.

checkpoint.prompt: A resident supports the clinic site. What does that support not establish?
options: That the outstanding permission for the temporary structure has been granted.
That access needs may differ from the priorities shown by footfall counts.
That residents can contribute relevant observations to the discussion.
checkpoint.note: Support and permission are distinct forms of evidence.

checkpoint.prompt: Averages improve but one access route becomes worse. Which report is most defensible?
options: Publish the average and the uneven effects, and consider revising the intervention.
Publish the average alone because subgroup findings must agree with it.
Treat the average as false solely because one subgroup experiences a drawback.
checkpoint.note: Overall and distributional findings can both be valid.

checkpoint.prompt: Why publish reasons to stop before the pilot begins?
options: To limit selective interpretation when the results include both benefits and drawbacks.
To guarantee that every measure will move in the same direction.
To make it unnecessary to record any unexpected adverse outcome.
checkpoint.note: Prior criteria help make the pilot a genuine test rather than a retrospective justification.

readingPoints: Describe the measured surface difference without claiming a proven reduction in personal exposure.
The basis for attributing an observed difference to the intervention.
They can overlook prolonged exposure among fewer people at waiting places.
Compare options over time, including their maintenance and changing shade coverage.
Which claims come from measurements, reported experiences or interpretation.
Run a proportionate pilot that reports distributions, drawbacks and grounds for revision.
listeningPoints: A desired journey-level benefit is not yet the demonstrated outcome.
Retained with its limitations, while other comparisons help address specific questions.
Its temporary structure still requires permission despite the decision to include the stop.
Investigate what each measure captures and retain the discrepancy in reporting.
Maintenance funding and responsibility, separate from fitting and removal.
Choosing a favourable outcome afterwards and presenting it as the original success criterion.

archives.title: Who becomes visible in a digital archive?
archives.goal: Interpret a digitisation proposal, distinguish searchability from completeness and negotiate responsible public access.
archives.role: a fictional archive curator consulting community representatives about a digitisation pilot
goals: Distinguish preserved material, searchable descriptions and historical representativeness.
Explain a privacy or consent boundary using the source evidence.
Propose a reversible access arrangement with a transparent correction process.
archives.opening: We can make more of this archive searchable, but visibility brings responsibilities. Whose needs should shape the pilot, and what should remain limited?

reading.prompt: Which distinction should guide the access project?
options: Improved searchability ensures that missing historical experiences are now represented.
A selection of surviving donations can be treated as a complete record once digitised.
Improved searchability does not establish that the collection represents everyone equally.
reading.note: Access to a collection and representativeness of that collection are different questions.

reading.prompt: Why preserve earlier catalogue versions when correcting an entry?
options: Silent replacement is necessary to make the collection’s history more transparent.
Researchers need to trace what changed and which version supported their work.
Earlier versions prove that the first automated transcription must have been correct.
reading.note: A correction should improve access without concealing the record of interpretation.

reading.prompt: What is the proposed purpose of a contextual note?
options: Distinguish historical wording from the archive’s present description without hiding its source.
Replace every historical document with language chosen by the current committee.
Present an older label as the archive’s unquestioned current description of a community.
reading.note: Context can preserve evidence while clarifying the institution’s descriptive choices.

reading.prompt: Which claim goes beyond the proposed access policy?
options: A preserved item may have a public description without an unrestricted online image.
A consultation request can be reviewed separately from general online publication.
Ownership of a donated letter automatically authorises unrestricted publication of every personal detail.
reading.note: Ownership, preservation and public disclosure do not carry identical permissions.

reading.prompt: Why examine unsuccessful searches?
options: They show that every popular image has been used for educational research.
They may reveal catalogue barriers or collection gaps that download totals overlook.
They establish that no relevant historical material could ever have existed.
reading.note: An unsuccessful search is informative, but its cause must still be examined.

reading.prompt: Which conclusion best preserves the proposal’s balance?
options: Expand access while documenting selection, interpretation and unresolved responsibilities.
Expand access by treating each searchable description as a neutral and complete historical fact.
Expand access by transferring all review responsibility to whoever downloads a document.
reading.note: The proposal combines access with visible, reviewable institutional choices.

listening.prompt: What must users know about the pilot’s scope?
options: It includes every neighbourhood document from the entire archive.
It establishes that unlisted groups were historically inactive.
Its defined selection limits what an absent search result can imply.
listening.note: The selected search corpus is narrower than the town’s history.

listening.prompt: Which statement preserves the review status accurately?
options: A visible uncertainty notice means the archive has discarded the original image.
Review of key fields does not mean that every transcribed line has been checked.
A checked title guarantees that all handwriting recognition is accurate.
listening.note: Describe the extent of checking rather than giving a blanket assurance.

listening.prompt: What does a submitted correction trigger?
options: A documented review rather than an immediate unexamined replacement.
An automatic public edit that cannot retain a previous version.
A guarantee that every disagreement will be settled within the target time.
listening.note: Participation and editorial responsibility are linked through the review process.

listening.prompt: Which inference should be avoided?
options: That public disclosure and ownership may need separate consideration.
That a limited description can be published while an access request is reviewed.
That delaying an unrestricted image means the document is no longer preserved or consultable in any form.
listening.note: A restriction on one access route does not settle every preservation or consultation decision.

listening.prompt: What risk does a download-only ranking create?
options: It prevents any popular document from being used more than once.
It may reinforce the visibility of collections already easiest to find.
It necessarily measures the needs of communities absent from the catalogue.
listening.note: Recorded popularity depends partly on existing visibility and access.

listening.prompt: Which response to a review-capacity problem is proposed?
options: Pause expansion while preserving appropriate access to material already reviewed.
Close every preserved collection permanently regardless of its review status.
Ignore the queue because any delay proves hostility to public access.
listening.note: A targeted pause can address the process without reversing every access decision.

roleplay.prompt: Our search returns nothing about one community. What can we responsibly say?
options: The absence of a result establishes that the community left no historical record anywhere.
The new search interface guarantees that all previously overlooked voices are represented.
The selected catalogue contains no result; we need to examine selection and description before inferring historical absence.
roleplay.note: Keep the search finding within the actual scope of the corpus.
roleplay.sceneLine: Our search returns nothing about one community. What can we responsibly say?

roleplay.prompt: A reviewer checked the document title. How should we label the transcription?
options: Remove all original images so users cannot notice transcription uncertainty.
Specify that key fields were reviewed and mark unreviewed text clearly.
Describe the complete transcription as verified because its title was checked.
roleplay.note: Communicate the granularity of verification.
roleplay.sceneLine: A reviewer checked the document title. How should we label the transcription?

roleplay.prompt: Two users disagree about a historical label. What process would you propose?
options: Retain the source wording with context and review reasoned challenges transparently.
Let the first user silently replace the catalogue and remove the previous wording.
Present the historical label as the institution’s current judgement without explanation.
roleplay.note: Separate preservation of wording from endorsement and record interpretive changes.
roleplay.sceneLine: Two users disagree about a historical label. What process would you propose?

roleplay.prompt: A donor wants immediate publication of a private letter. What should we clarify?
options: Ownership eliminates every question concerning living people mentioned in a letter.
A delayed online image requires the physical letter to be destroyed.
Ownership and unrestricted disclosure require separate consideration, including other people’s circumstances.
roleplay.note: Distinguish the decisions instead of treating access as an all-or-nothing choice.
roleplay.sceneLine: A donor wants immediate publication of a private letter. What should we clarify?

roleplay.prompt: The most downloaded collection asks for all next year’s funding. What concern would you raise?
options: A popular collection must have no educational value and should lose all access.
Existing visibility may shape downloads, so we should also examine unmet needs and collection gaps.
Download totals independently establish the complete historical importance of every collection.
roleplay.note: Question the ranking’s scope without dismissing all evidence of demand.
roleplay.sceneLine: The most downloaded collection asks for all next year’s funding. What concern would you raise?

roleplay.prompt: Correction requests exceed our capacity. What is a proportionate next step?
options: Pause expansion, resource the review queue and keep appropriately reviewed material available.
Expand faster while treating every unresolved correction as automatically wrong.
Close all research access permanently to avoid explaining the review process.
roleplay.note: A bounded operational response can protect both access and trust.
roleplay.sceneLine: Correction requests exceed our capacity. What is a proportionate next step?

checkpoint.prompt: Which difference is essential to evaluating the project’s reach?
options: The difference between a document’s popularity and its automatically verified completeness.
The difference between identical collections displayed under two unrelated search buttons.
The difference between searchable surviving holdings and a representative history of the town.
checkpoint.note: Searchable access cannot recreate experiences missing from the holdings.

checkpoint.prompt: Which assurance would the curator refuse to give?
options: That an approved original image can help users inspect a difficult reading.
That checking a title verifies every line of the automated transcription.
That unreviewed text should have a visible notice.
checkpoint.note: The described review has a limited scope.

checkpoint.prompt: Why retain a contextual note with an older term?
options: To show the term’s source and distinguish historical wording from current description.
To establish that every older label remains the archive’s preferred modern description.
To remove the possibility of any future challenge to descriptive choices.
checkpoint.note: Context can preserve evidence and make interpretive responsibility visible.

checkpoint.prompt: What does the correction target time not guarantee?
options: Resolution of every difficult disagreement within that period.
Entry of a submitted correction into a review process.
A revision date and explanation for an accepted change.
checkpoint.note: A service target is not an unconditional outcome promise.

checkpoint.prompt: Which evidence would challenge a claim based solely on high download totals?
options: A published explanation of why one collection was selected for the pilot.
Repeated failed searches from communities whose material remains hard to discover.
The existence of an approved image available beside a transcription.
checkpoint.note: Visibility and unmet need matter alongside recorded demand.

checkpoint.prompt: Which recommendation integrates access and responsible operation?
options: Expand at a pace that supports sensitive-material review and traceable corrections.
Treat any pause in expansion as proof that every existing access decision was mistaken.
Publish all images first and make every affected person prove why review was needed later.
checkpoint.note: The pilot aims for accountable access rather than expansion detached from review capacity.

readingPoints: Improved searchability does not establish that the collection represents everyone equally.
Researchers need to trace what changed and which version supported their work.
Distinguish historical wording from the archive’s present description without hiding its source.
Ownership of a donated letter automatically authorises unrestricted publication of every personal detail.
They may reveal catalogue barriers or collection gaps that download totals overlook.
Expand access while documenting selection, interpretation and unresolved responsibilities.
listeningPoints: Its defined selection limits what an absent search result can imply.
Review of key fields does not mean that every transcribed line has been checked.
A documented review rather than an immediate unexamined replacement.
That delaying an unrestricted image means the document is no longer preserved or consultable in any form.
It may reinforce the visibility of collections already easiest to find.
Pause expansion while preserving appropriate access to material already reviewed.

research.title: Evidence, funding and the claims we can make
research.goal: Critically compare a research summary and an interview, identify alternative explanations and negotiate a proportionate next study.
research.role: a fictional research-panel chair deciding how to evaluate a community transport pilot
goals: Distinguish observed association from an identified causal effect.
Explain which uncertainty a proposed design change could address.
Recommend a proportionate funding decision with explicit limits.
research.opening: The pilot results look encouraging, but our next funding decision should depend on what they actually establish. Which claim needs the most careful qualification?

reading.prompt: Which wording best matches the reported evidence?
options: Registered users had higher attendance, which identifies the shuttle’s independent effect for all learners.
Registered users had higher attendance, so their earlier attendance is irrelevant to any interpretation.
Registered users had higher attendance, but the comparison alone does not identify the shuttle’s effect.
reading.note: Selection and missing baseline information leave alternative explanations open.

reading.prompt: What distinction should the panel preserve?
options: A larger passenger total removes the need to understand differences between the groups.
Operational reliability data and evidence of an attendance effect answer different questions.
Detailed departure records directly reveal every non-user’s reason for not registering.
reading.note: More data are useful only when their relationship to the question is made explicit.

reading.prompt: Which inference would the article reject?
options: An uncertain effect estimate establishes that the shuttle provides no benefit.
Interrupting the service may impose a burden not captured by the initial comparison.
The funding decision can involve practical consequences as well as research quality.
reading.note: Failure to identify an effect is different from evidence of no effect.

reading.prompt: How should the proposed evaluation options be compared?
options: By assuming that any baseline measure eliminates all possible alternative explanations.
By treating a transparent allocation rule as automatically appropriate in every setting.
By the uncertainties each addresses and the practical or ethical constraints each introduces.
reading.note: A stronger design still needs a question-specific and proportionate justification.

reading.prompt: Why might the panel prefer a higher weekly price?
options: A discount proves that the operational and evaluation objectives have already been agreed.
A shorter commitment could preserve options while the evaluation question is clarified.
A higher weekly price necessarily makes the total annual commitment smaller in every scenario.
reading.note: Unit price should be considered alongside commitment and the ability to adapt.

reading.prompt: Which conclusion best reflects the proposed recommendation?
options: Continue temporarily for stated practical reasons while evaluating the effect without overstating it.
Commit for a full year because the initial group difference has already settled causation.
End the service because uncertainty removes any legitimate practical reason to continue it.
reading.note: A provisional policy decision can be explicit about both its rationale and evidential limits.

listening.prompt: What exactly is the panel questioning?
options: The existence of every passenger record, rather than the interpretation of the attendance figures.
The possibility that practical access could matter to any learner attending evening classes.
The causal inference drawn from the group comparison, rather than the existence of the records.
listening.note: A criticism of inference should not be expanded into an allegation about data fabrication.

listening.prompt: What condition matters when using earlier records?
options: A requirement to discard all earlier records whenever one definition differs.
Comparability of the attendance definitions as well as the conditions for using the records.
The assumption that every historical attendance figure uses an identical definition.
listening.note: The researcher proposes qualified use, not unquestioned pooling or blanket rejection.

listening.prompt: How should the extension currently be described?
options: A proposed three-month arrangement with contract and access conditions still outstanding.
A signed full-year arrangement because the operator has agreed to discuss a shorter term.
An unconditional three-month guarantee that no longer requires accessible transport planning.
listening.note: Discussion and conditional approval are not the same as a completed commitment.

listening.prompt: Which limit applies to the allocation idea?
options: It authorises removing all existing users before any further review is necessary.
It guarantees that a research comparison overrides every service entitlement.
It concerns possible excess new demand and remains subject to review of access and rights.
listening.note: The speaker restricts both the proposed population and its authorisation status.

listening.prompt: What safeguard does the chair propose?
options: Interpret every attendance change without checking whether the shuttle actually operated.
Specify relevant contextual records in advance rather than invent explanations only after the result.
Keep adding unplanned explanations until every possible unfavourable result can be dismissed.
listening.note: Pre-specification helps distinguish planned interpretation from selective excuse-making.

listening.prompt: What basis for public confidence does the chair advocate?
options: Clear reasons, limits and future decision criteria rather than an unqualified success claim.
An assurance that funding has removed all uncertainty from the effect estimate.
A commitment to expansion regardless of what the evaluation later finds.
listening.note: The chair locates confidence in accountable decision-making.

roleplay.prompt: The team wants the headline “The shuttle improved attendance.” What wording would you defend?
options: The higher user attendance proves the same causal benefit for every future learner.
The absence of a baseline proves that the service did not affect any learner.
Users had higher attendance in this pilot, but the comparison does not isolate the service’s effect.
roleplay.note: Retain the finding while qualifying the inference.
roleplay.sceneLine: The team wants the headline “The shuttle improved attendance.” What wording would you defend?

roleplay.prompt: A colleague says that detailed journey logs settle the attendance question. How would you respond?
options: Because the logs are useful, no information about registration can matter.
They show how the service ran; we still need to examine the comparison between learners.
The logs directly show what each learner would have done without the service.
roleplay.note: Match the evidence to the question being asked.
roleplay.sceneLine: A colleague says that detailed journey logs settle the attendance question. How would you respond?

roleplay.prompt: An immediate annual contract offers a lower weekly price. What else should the panel weigh?
options: Total commitment, access conditions and the value of retaining options while evaluating.
Only the weekly price, because commitment length cannot affect the decision.
Only the operator’s enthusiasm, because a discount identifies the causal effect.
roleplay.note: A financial decision includes option value and delivery conditions.
roleplay.sceneLine: An immediate annual contract offers a lower weekly price. What else should the panel weigh?

roleplay.prompt: Can we allocate existing users away from the shuttle for a cleaner comparison?
options: A more informative comparison automatically overrides every existing entitlement.
A research aim establishes that the service is unnecessary for current users.
That is not the current proposal; existing access and rights need separate consideration.
roleplay.note: Do not generalise a conditional proposal about new excess demand.
roleplay.sceneLine: Can we allocate existing users away from the shuttle for a cleaner comparison?

roleplay.prompt: Earlier attendance records use different definitions. What should the study do?
options: Assume that all historical attendance records must be fabricated.
Explain and assess comparability before combining them with the new records.
Combine them silently because a larger dataset is always more valid.
roleplay.note: More observations do not remove measurement differences.
roleplay.sceneLine: Earlier attendance records use different definitions. What should the study do?

roleplay.prompt: Please state a defensible funding recommendation.
options: Offer a bounded extension with clear access conditions and pre-specified evaluation milestones.
Guarantee a year of funding because the first report used a positive headline.
Reject any further service provision because no effect size has been isolated.
roleplay.note: A proportionate decision can acknowledge need and uncertainty together.
roleplay.sceneLine: Please state a defensible funding recommendation.

checkpoint.prompt: Which missing information could help examine selection into the shuttle group?
options: The assumption that all non-users faced identical travel conditions.
Comparable prior attendance and reasons for registration or non-registration.
The number of publicity photographs taken on the first operating evening.
checkpoint.note: Selection concerns the people being compared.

checkpoint.prompt: What does revising the success headline not imply?
options: That a group difference can be reported with appropriate qualification.
That a causal inference requires more than the observed comparison alone.
That the panel has found the operational records were fabricated.
checkpoint.note: The interview explicitly separates inference from fabrication.

checkpoint.prompt: Why can practical need justify considering a temporary extension?
options: A policy decision can weigh interruption costs while remaining explicit about uncertain effects.
Practical need automatically converts an observational comparison into a causal experiment.
Temporary funding guarantees that every learner would otherwise miss all classes.
checkpoint.note: Decision justification and effect identification are related but distinct.

checkpoint.prompt: Which fact would be omitted by announcing a guaranteed extension now?
options: The operator has only agreed to discuss the term, and accessible transport still needs confirmation.
The proposed term is shorter than the full-year contract initially requested.
The panel plans to review evidence before a further commitment.
checkpoint.note: Material conditions are still outstanding.

checkpoint.prompt: Which comparison best addresses the contract choice?
options: The amount of publicity alone, treating it as a measure of service effectiveness.
Weekly cost together with total commitment and the ability to revise the plan.
Weekly cost alone, treating every contract duration as equivalent.
checkpoint.note: The article makes commitment and flexibility relevant.

checkpoint.prompt: What would distinguish planned contextual analysis from an excuse after the event?
options: Promising that contextual information can never change interpretation.
Recording relevant factors and decision criteria before observing the outcome.
Adding explanations only when a result threatens the preferred decision.
checkpoint.note: The interview advocates advance specification.

readingPoints: Registered users had higher attendance, but the comparison alone does not identify the shuttle’s effect.
Operational reliability data and evidence of an attendance effect answer different questions.
An uncertain effect estimate establishes that the shuttle provides no benefit.
By the uncertainties each addresses and the practical or ethical constraints each introduces.
A shorter commitment could preserve options while the evaluation question is clarified.
Continue temporarily for stated practical reasons while evaluating the effect without overstating it.
listeningPoints: The causal inference drawn from the group comparison, rather than the existence of the records.
Comparability of the attendance definitions as well as the conditions for using the records.
A proposed three-month arrangement with contract and access conditions still outstanding.
It concerns possible excess new demand and remains subject to review of access and rights.
Specify relevant contextual records in advance rather than invent explanations only after the result.
Clear reasons, limits and future decision criteria rather than an unqualified success claim.

heritage.title: Whose heritage, and who decides?
heritage.goal: Compare accounts of a restoration project, distinguish physical preservation from cultural participation and negotiate a reviewable agreement.
heritage.role: a fictional community facilitator discussing the future use of a restored waterfront hall
goals: Represent the different meanings attached to the hall.
Distinguish consultation, permission and a continuing decision-making role.
Propose a workable agreement on access, funding and future review.
heritage.opening: The waterfront hall can be restored, but agreement about the building is not agreement about its future use. Which commitments should be settled before work begins?

reading.prompt: What is the central distinction in the disagreement?
options: Support for informal gatherings means every community group opposes repairing the building.
Agreement on the building’s condition automatically settles who should control its programme.
Agreement on physical repair does not establish agreement on the hall’s future cultural use.
reading.note: Different dimensions of heritage can be valued while repair itself is widely supported.

reading.prompt: Why might a large total of community-access hours be misleading?
options: Working residents can always replace an evening visit with a weekday morning visit.
The available times may be unusable for many of the people meant to benefit.
A larger access-hour total necessarily gives residents control over every evening event.
reading.note: The distribution and conditions of access matter as well as its total duration.

reading.prompt: Which approach does the historian support?
options: Acknowledge different periods and contested memories without erasing the hall’s origins.
Select one period as authentic and exclude every later use from the account.
Treat all disagreement as evidence that the hall has no meaningful history.
reading.note: A layered history can recognise origins without fixing culture at one moment.

reading.prompt: What would make the consultation record more reliable?
options: Treat attendance as approval of every later funding and management condition.
Remove objections so the public record presents a single apparently agreed position.
Specify what participants were asked and separate suggestions from approval of unpresented terms.
reading.note: The scope of participation constrains what consent can be inferred.

reading.prompt: Why must the committee’s powers be specified?
options: An advisory body cannot provide any useful knowledge under any circumstances.
Membership alone does not show which decisions participants can actually influence.
A committee seat automatically grants equal control over every budget and programme decision.
reading.note: Representation and formal decision-making authority should not be conflated.

reading.prompt: Which conclusion best reflects the recommendation?
options: Link restoration to a specified, reviewable arrangement for operation and meaningful access.
Treat ticketed attendance as a complete measure of every form of public benefit.
Require every future activity to reproduce exactly one earlier period of use.
reading.note: The recommendation combines viable operation with accountable cultural access.

listening.prompt: What is the current approval status?
options: Unconditional restoration funding and a final operating agreement approved together.
A refusal to permit any further design work until every future event is booked.
A conditional funding offer and permission for further design work, with the operating agreement unresolved.
listening.note: The interview separates different approvals and retains outstanding conditions.

listening.prompt: What remains to be settled about the evening slots?
options: Whether a numerical total automatically proves access is adequate.
Their usable scheduling pattern and fee arrangements.
Whether any evening slots appear in the revised draft at all.
listening.note: A reserved total still leaves important conditions unresolved.

listening.prompt: How will differing memories be handled?
options: Attributed and compared with records, with uncertainty made visible.
Combined into one exact account with disagreements silently removed.
Excluded entirely because recollections cannot contribute useful evidence.
listening.note: The historian supports contextualised evidence rather than forced unanimity.

listening.prompt: Which authority does the current draft provide?
options: Complete control of the foundation’s budget through an advisory committee seat.
A final decision on every contract merely because residents attend the meeting.
Programming advice and access to an annual access report, rather than budget control.
listening.note: Describe existing draft powers separately from powers people may seek.

listening.prompt: What qualification applies to the reduced-fee route?
options: It requires applicants to disclose private circumstances publicly before they can ask.
It is proposed, with the allocation and accessible application process still to be settled.
It guarantees unlimited free access to every group without further agreement.
listening.note: The support route is a commitment to develop, not an unlimited existing entitlement.

listening.prompt: What cannot be established from attendance alone?
options: Whether access, representation and maintenance arrangements meet the wider aims.
Whether any recorded visit or ticket count exists under the stated method.
Whether a busy building may provide some genuine opportunities for participation.
listening.note: Attendance is relevant evidence with a limited scope.

roleplay.prompt: The press says that funding and operation are fully approved. What correction would you recommend?
options: Describe the design approval as authority for every future booking and management decision.
Treat the existence of an offer as proof that every funding condition has been satisfied.
Distinguish the conditional offer and design approval from the unresolved operating agreement.
roleplay.note: Separate stages of commitment and approval.
roleplay.sceneLine: The press says that funding and operation are fully approved. What correction would you recommend?

roleplay.prompt: Two community evenings a month look sufficient on paper. What would you ask next?
options: Whether working residents can simply replace every evening activity with a morning one.
Which evenings, at what cost, and whether the intended groups can actually attend.
Whether a monthly total removes the need to examine time or affordability.
roleplay.note: Meaningful access depends on practical conditions as well as the count.
roleplay.sceneLine: Two community evenings a month look sufficient on paper. What would you ask next?

roleplay.prompt: Should we remove conflicting memories to make the exhibition easier to understand?
options: We can attribute the accounts, compare sources and explain uncertainty without forcing agreement.
We should silently choose whichever account best supports the funding announcement.
We should exclude every recollection because records can never require interpretation.
roleplay.note: Clarity can come from explaining differences rather than suppressing them.
roleplay.sceneLine: Should we remove conflicting memories to make the exhibition easier to understand?

roleplay.prompt: A resident assumes their committee seat gives budget control. How would you clarify the draft?
options: An advisory seat already gives each resident full control over the foundation’s finances.
The draft proves that no resident can ever seek a stronger decision-making role.
It currently provides advice and an access report; stronger powers would need to be negotiated.
roleplay.note: State present authority without closing legitimate negotiation.
roleplay.sceneLine: A resident assumes their committee seat gives budget control. How would you clarify the draft?

roleplay.prompt: Can we promise unlimited free use to groups that cannot pay?
options: No, because asking for help automatically disqualifies a group from every booking.
Not on the current draft; we need a funded allocation and a fair application route.
Yes, proposing a reduced-fee route establishes unlimited free capacity.
roleplay.note: Keep the promise proportionate to the actual commitment.
roleplay.sceneLine: Can we promise unlimited free use to groups that cannot pay?

roleplay.prompt: What condition would you attach to the first-year review?
options: Include groups unable to book and displaced activities alongside attendance and maintenance.
Treat high attendance as proof that every cultural-access aim has been met.
Review only events that received favourable publicity from the foundation.
roleplay.note: A review should examine excluded experiences as well as visible use.
roleplay.sceneLine: What condition would you attach to the first-year review?

checkpoint.prompt: Which agreement cannot be inferred from shared support for repair?
options: Agreement that the building has physical deterioration worth addressing.
Agreement that further discussion of the hall’s future is relevant.
Agreement on future use, access and the distribution of decision-making power.
checkpoint.note: A shared repair aim does not settle the wider operating model.

checkpoint.prompt: Which detail qualifies the proposed evening-access promise?
options: The revised draft grants unlimited free use on any evening residents choose.
The exact days and fees remain to be agreed despite the reserved monthly total.
No evening slots appear in any version of the proposal.
checkpoint.note: The interview specifies both progress and unresolved practical conditions.

checkpoint.prompt: Why document the consultation questions?
options: To convert every suggestion automatically into approval of later contractual terms.
To establish that attending a meeting removes the right to object afterwards.
To limit claims of consent to what participants were actually invited to consider.
checkpoint.note: The scope of consultation determines the scope of defensible inferences.

checkpoint.prompt: Which statement accurately describes the current committee proposal?
options: It already controls every financial decision because residents would hold seats.
It cannot receive any information because advisory bodies have no possible role.
It is advisory on programming and can receive an annual access report, without budget control.
checkpoint.note: Representation, information rights and budget authority are distinct.

checkpoint.prompt: What would make an attendance-based success claim incomplete?
options: It omits people unable to book and activities displaced by the new programme.
It acknowledges that some real use of the hall has occurred.
It describes the method used to count recorded visits.
checkpoint.note: Visible attendance cannot capture every access and participation outcome.

checkpoint.prompt: Which final recommendation best integrates the two accounts?
options: Proceed with explicit operating, access and review commitments while retaining unresolved conditions honestly.
Treat a conditional funding offer as enough to settle every concern about use.
Delay explaining access conditions until groups have organised activities around a fixed opening date.
checkpoint.note: A viable restoration depends on clear, reviewable arrangements beyond physical repair.

readingPoints: Agreement on physical repair does not establish agreement on the hall’s future cultural use.
The available times may be unusable for many of the people meant to benefit.
Acknowledge different periods and contested memories without erasing the hall’s origins.
Specify what participants were asked and separate suggestions from approval of unpresented terms.
Membership alone does not show which decisions participants can actually influence.
Link restoration to a specified, reviewable arrangement for operation and meaningful access.
listeningPoints: A conditional funding offer and permission for further design work, with the operating agreement unresolved.
Their usable scheduling pattern and fee arrangements.
Attributed and compared with records, with uncertainty made visible.
Programming advice and access to an annual access report, rather than budget control.
It is proposed, with the allocation and accessible application process still to be settled.
Whether access, representation and maintenance arrangements meet the wider aims.

market.title: A market that works for everyone
market.goal: Follow a neighbourhood proposal, compare practical needs and agree on a small trial.
market.role: the organiser of a fictional neighbourhood market discussing a six-week trial with a resident
