goals: Explain a resident’s concern using a detail from the article.
Compare the organiser’s update with the original plan.
Agree on a practical trial and a way to review it.
market.opening: Thanks for coming. We want the Saturday market to work for neighbours as well as visitors. What should we change first?

reading.prompt: What is the purpose of the proposal?
options: To move all twelve stalls into the park.
To make the market a permanent evening event.
To test a later closing time for six weeks.
reading.note: The later closing time is a temporary proposal; it has not been made permanent.

reading.prompt: What does Leila support?
options: An earlier start for the bakery.
More time to shop after work.
Live music throughout the afternoon.
reading.note: Leila separates longer shopping hours from continuous music.

reading.prompt: Why does Arun ask for a clear path?
options: His mother needs enough space to walk safely.
He wants to park delivery vans there all day.
He believes the market should close completely.
reading.note: The requested space concerns access, not a demand to remove the market.

reading.prompt: What limit would visitors need to understand?
options: Every seller must remain until six.
No stalls would open in the morning.
Only some stalls may stay open later.
reading.note: Optional extra hours mean the afternoon selection may be smaller.

reading.prompt: Why ask people who do not shop at the market?
options: They have already agreed to the new schedule.
They may be affected even if they are not customers.
Their answers can replace all access checks.
reading.note: The people affected include neighbours outside the customer group.

reading.prompt: Which conclusion best matches the plan?
options: Review several kinds of evidence before keeping the change.
Keep the change automatically if customer numbers rise.
Return to the old hours without asking anyone.
reading.note: The final decision considers benefits and practical costs together.

listening.prompt: Has the later opening already begun?
options: Yes; it has already become permanent.
Yes; it finished six weeks ago.
No; the group still has to decide whether to start the trial.
listening.note: The organiser describes planning, not a completed trial.

listening.prompt: What should visitors check on Friday?
options: The price of every item in the bakery.
The final list of sellers offering extra hours.
A promise that all twelve sellers will stay.
listening.note: Seven expressions of interest do not establish the final list.

listening.prompt: What is the revised delivery proposal?
options: One possible earlier bread delivery through the rear entrance.
All vans can use the front pavement before seven.
Every delivery has been moved to seven thirty.
listening.note: The exception is limited and still needs consultation.

listening.prompt: How would volunteers handle a heavy box on the route?
options: Carry every heavy box without help.
Leave the route blocked until six.
Ask the responsible stallholder to move it.
listening.note: The plan assigns responsibility without requiring unsafe lifting.

listening.prompt: What does the rule after four concern?
options: A requirement for every seller to play music.
Amplified music, rather than ordinary conversation.
A complete ban on speaking.
listening.note: The organiser distinguishes a sound system from normal conversation.

listening.prompt: What can a volunteer offer?
options: One afternoon, with clear availability.
A promise to attend all six weeks whether possible or not.
Only money; no practical help is accepted.
listening.note: The organiser explicitly accepts a limited but realistic commitment.

roleplay.prompt: A neighbour says that opposing loud music means opposing the market. How do you respond?
options: Then everyone who dislikes music must stay home.
There is no need to hear any other concern.
We can support the market while asking for quieter activities.
roleplay.note: Distinguish the market’s purpose from one type of activity.
roleplay.sceneLine: A neighbour says that opposing loud music means opposing the market. How do you respond?

roleplay.prompt: I work alone at my stall and cannot stay every Saturday. What would you suggest?
options: Your morning stall must close because of that.
Could you choose the afternoons you can manage and publish them?
You should promise to stay even when you cannot.
roleplay.note: A feasible option respects optional extra hours.
roleplay.sceneLine: I work alone at my stall and cannot stay every Saturday. What would you suggest?

roleplay.prompt: We have seven interested sellers. Can we advertise that all twelve will stay?
options: Let us wait for Friday’s final list before making that claim.
Yes, interest from seven proves all twelve have agreed.
We should say that no one is interested.
roleplay.note: Keep expressions of interest separate from confirmed participation.
roleplay.sceneLine: We have seven interested sellers. Can we advertise that all twelve will stay?

roleplay.prompt: The earlier bread delivery might help the bakery. What should we check?
options: Whether every delivery can ignore the proposed hours.
Whether we can avoid telling the residents.
How the rear delivery would affect the nearby residents.
roleplay.note: Consult the people affected by the exception.
roleplay.sceneLine: The earlier bread delivery might help the bakery. What should we check?

roleplay.prompt: Customer numbers went up. Is that enough to keep the new hours?
options: No, more customers must mean the trial failed.
We should also review noise, access and the workload.
Yes, customer numbers answer every question.
roleplay.note: Combine evidence about benefits and costs.
roleplay.sceneLine: Customer numbers went up. Is that enough to keep the new hours?

roleplay.prompt: Can you help with the trial? Please make a realistic offer.
options: I can check the route next Saturday afternoon; who should I contact?
I will attend every day, although I know I am unavailable.
I will decide what everyone else must do without asking.
roleplay.note: A specific offer and a follow-up question help the plan move forward.
roleplay.sceneLine: Can you help with the trial? Please make a realistic offer.

checkpoint.prompt: Which response respects both Leila’s and Arun’s needs?
options: Extend shopping and remove every delivery restriction.
Offer later shopping while protecting quiet and clear access.
Cancel the market because they have different priorities.
checkpoint.note: Their concerns can be addressed together.

checkpoint.prompt: Which detail in the interview changes the article’s delivery plan?
options: A possible bread delivery at seven thirty through the rear entrance.
A confirmed move of every delivery to seven thirty.
A decision to stop selling bread altogether.
checkpoint.note: The interview proposes one limited exception.

checkpoint.prompt: Why would a seller’s name be missing from the afternoon list?
options: The morning market has been cancelled.
Every seller has agreed to remain until six.
Extra hours are optional, and availability may differ.
checkpoint.note: The smaller afternoon selection follows from optional participation.

checkpoint.prompt: A post says that people cannot talk after four. Which correction is accurate?
options: Only customers can speak after four.
The proposed restriction concerns amplified music.
Every sound is forbidden after four.
checkpoint.note: Do not expand a music restriction into a ban on conversation.

checkpoint.prompt: What would make the final report incomplete?
options: Reporting customer numbers without access or noise evidence.
Including feedback from people who do not shop there.
Recording the workload of volunteers.
checkpoint.note: The plan needs several kinds of evidence.

checkpoint.prompt: You cannot attend Monday’s meeting. What can you still do?
options: Assume that silence counts as a vote for permanent hours.
Ask a seller to invent your opinion.
Leave a written comment at the library.
checkpoint.note: The interview gives an alternative way to contribute.

readingPoints: To test a later closing time for six weeks.
More time to shop after work.
His mother needs enough space to walk safely.
Only some stalls may stay open later.
They may be affected even if they are not customers.
Review several kinds of evidence before keeping the change.
listeningPoints: No; the group still has to decide whether to start the trial.
The final list of sellers offering extra hours.
One possible earlier bread delivery through the rear entrance.
Ask the responsible stallholder to move it.
Amplified music, rather than ordinary conversation.
One afternoon, with clear availability.

library.title: An evening library for the neighbourhood
library.goal: Follow a service change, interpret an updated announcement and agree on an accessible plan.
library.role: a fictional librarian arranging a limited evening opening with a local resident
goals: Explain who could benefit from evening access.
Clarify the updated booking and staffing arrangements.
Agree on a useful next step without promising an unavailable service.
library.opening: We are planning a small evening library trial. Who do you think would use it, and what would they need?

reading.prompt: What is being proposed?
options: A permanent change to every weekday evening.
A requirement that staff work without pay.
One later opening each week for a two-month trial.
reading.note: The proposal is limited in both frequency and duration.

reading.prompt: Why might the two activities need separate areas?
options: Language learners are not allowed in libraries.
A conversation group could disturb quiet study.
Nora has asked for a new computer in every room.
reading.note: Both uses are welcome, but their sound needs differ.

reading.prompt: What would a conversation group need to do?
options: Book the smaller room and name an organiser.
Use any space without telling the library.
Ask all quiet readers to leave the building.
reading.note: The booking creates a defined space and responsibility.

reading.prompt: Which service would remain unavailable during the trial evening?
options: The lift and step-free entrance.
Borrowing ordinary books.
Access to the upstairs archive.
reading.note: The limitation concerns specialist archive access, not the entrance.

reading.prompt: What is the proposed role of volunteers?
options: Keep the library open alone if staff cannot attend.
Help with directions while paid staff handle protected records.
Replace absent staff and access everyone’s borrowing history.
reading.note: The proposal sets a clear boundary around volunteer duties.

reading.prompt: Why ask how visitors heard about the trial?
options: Low attendance might partly reflect limited awareness.
It would prove that all residents use social media.
It would replace every other measure of the service.
reading.note: The same attendance figure can have more than one explanation.

listening.prompt: Which date should residents use?
options: The first Wednesday shown on the old poster.
Every evening from the start of the month.
The second Wednesday of next month.
listening.note: The new announcement replaces the earlier date.

listening.prompt: What must be settled before the group booking is confirmed?
options: Whether three groups can all use the room separately at once.
Who will be the main contact for a single booking.
Which group can take over the quiet room as well.
listening.note: Interest is not the same as a confirmed room booking.

listening.prompt: Who is asked to contact the library beforehand?
options: Someone who needs a particular accessible arrangement.
Every visitor who wants to read any book.
Only people who already organise the language exchange.
listening.note: Ordinary tables are unreserved; specific access needs can be discussed.

listening.prompt: When might a computer session be extended?
options: Whenever a visitor asks, even with a queue.
Only if the visitor becomes a volunteer.
When no one is waiting and staff agree.
listening.note: The extension is conditional, not an automatic entitlement.

listening.prompt: Who should answer a question about a borrowing account?
options: Another reader who knows the borrower.
A member of library staff.
Any volunteer who happens to be near the entrance.
listening.note: Account information stays with authorised staff.

listening.prompt: What should the feedback-form total represent?
options: The number of submitted forms, not every library visitor.
A complete count of everyone in the building.
A list of named borrowing accounts.
listening.note: Optional feedback does not cover all visitors.

roleplay.prompt: A visitor wants to practise speaking beside Nora’s study table. What could you suggest?
options: Everyone studying quietly should leave immediately.
Talking loudly is the only way to use an evening library.
Let us check whether the smaller room has been booked for conversation.
roleplay.note: Look for a space that respects both activities.
roleplay.sceneLine: A visitor wants to practise speaking beside Nora’s study table. What could you suggest?

roleplay.prompt: Three people each think they have organised the same exchange. How do you clarify it?
options: No one needs to tell the library who is responsible.
Could we agree on one main contact and confirm a single booking?
Let us promise the room to all three independently.
roleplay.note: A shared plan needs one clear booking.
roleplay.sceneLine: Three people each think they have organised the same exchange. How do you clarify it?

roleplay.prompt: I saw a poster saying the trial starts on the first Wednesday. Is that right?
options: The updated announcement says the second Wednesday.
Yes, the old poster is more reliable than the correction.
The trial has already ended.
roleplay.note: Use the corrected date rather than repeating the earlier notice.
roleplay.sceneLine: I saw a poster saying the trial starts on the first Wednesday. Is that right?

roleplay.prompt: May I use a computer for an hour?
options: An hour is guaranteed because the library is open later.
I will take over two computers for thirty minutes each.
Could we ask staff whether an extension is possible if no one is waiting?
roleplay.note: A request should retain the stated condition.
roleplay.sceneLine: May I use a computer for an hour?

roleplay.prompt: A volunteer offers to check a friend’s borrowing history for me. What should I do?
options: Post the account details where other visitors can see them.
Ask an authorised staff member about the correct process instead.
Accept because all volunteers can access private records.
roleplay.note: Welcoming duties do not grant access to private records.
roleplay.sceneLine: A volunteer offers to check a friend’s borrowing history for me. What should I do?

roleplay.prompt: Only six feedback forms were returned. What should we say in the report?
options: Six forms were returned; that does not tell us the total attendance.
Exactly six people used the library.
Everyone who did not complete a form disliked the trial.
roleplay.note: State what the measure actually records.
roleplay.sceneLine: Only six feedback forms were returned. What should we say in the report?

checkpoint.prompt: Which plan could support both quiet reading and a language exchange?
options: Keep the conversation group in the booked smaller room.
Require everyone in the reading room to join the exchange.
Treat the same table as a quiet and noisy space at once.
checkpoint.note: The rooms can meet different needs.

checkpoint.prompt: A friend plans to arrive on the first Wednesday. What information should you pass on?
options: The first date is unchanged because it appeared on a poster.
The building will be open every night.
The start has been corrected to the second Wednesday.
checkpoint.note: The updated announcement takes precedence.

checkpoint.prompt: Why does a later opening not guarantee archive access?
options: The step-free entrance is being removed.
All books must stay upstairs after five.
The evening service does not include an archive specialist.
checkpoint.note: A general opening time does not establish every specialist service.

checkpoint.prompt: Which description of computer access preserves the announcement’s meaning?
options: One hour for every visitor without exceptions.
No computer access is possible in the evening.
Thirty minutes normally; a longer session may be agreed if no one waits.
checkpoint.note: Preserve both the normal limit and the conditional extension.

checkpoint.prompt: What would help interpret low attendance fairly?
options: Check whether the intended users knew about the trial.
Assume the service was widely advertised without checking.
Ignore comments from people who could not attend.
checkpoint.note: Awareness is one possible explanation to investigate.

checkpoint.prompt: Which statement about the feedback form is accurate?
options: It is optional and can be anonymous unless a reply is requested.
Every visitor must provide a name.
It gives volunteers access to borrowing histories.
checkpoint.note: The interview describes optional feedback and a paper alternative.

readingPoints: One later opening each week for a two-month trial.
A conversation group could disturb quiet study.
Book the smaller room and name an organiser.
Access to the upstairs archive.
Help with directions while paid staff handle protected records.
Low attendance might partly reflect limited awareness.
listeningPoints: The second Wednesday of next month.
Who will be the main contact for a single booking.
Someone who needs a particular accessible arrangement.
When no one is waiting and staff agree.
A member of library staff.
The number of submitted forms, not every library visitor.
